meta.ogDescription: Really H.G. Wells — verified in his final book, The Mind at the End of its Tether (1945). Often stripped of its bleak original context.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Wells wrote this line in his final book, “The Mind at the End of its Tether” (1945), Section IV — confirmed word-for-word against the full text and matched by Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ (p. 19). The original capitalizes “Nature’s”; the popular lower-case form is the only real difference.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Mind at the End of its Tether

source.excerpt: There is no way out for Man but steeply up or steeply down. Adapt or perish, now as ever, is Nature’s inexorable imperative.
trail: The full text of The Mind at the End of its Tether ↗ carries the sentence verbatim in Section IV, and uses “Adapt or perish” again earlier: “Adapt or perish has been the inexorable law of life…”
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced section, citing the 1945 book, p. 19 — not among misattributed or disputed quotes.

Quote Investigator’s adaptation investigation ↗ traces a different line (“It is not the strongest of the species that survives…”) to a 1963 Megginson lecture misattributed to Darwin — a reminder that not every “adapt” aphorism is Wells’s.
source.excerptNote: The line closes a passage arguing that any successor to humanity “will certainly not be human” — the aphorism is delivered not as motivation but as a verdict on our species’ prospects.

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in 1945, so under U.S. copyright rules a work first published in or after 1931 remains in copyright, held by the Wells estate and its publisher. (In the U.K., where copyright runs life-plus-70, Wells’s works entered the public domain at the end of 2016; U.S. status is the more conservative and controlling one here.)

author.name: H.G. Wells
author.heading: About H.G. Wells
author.metaLine: 1866–1946 · English novelist, historian & futurist — “father of science fiction”
author.bio: Herbert George Wells was one of the most influential English writers of his era, author of The Time Machine, The War of the Worlds and The Invisible Man, plus sweeping works of history and social prophecy. This line comes from The Mind at the End of its Tether (1945), the bleak pamphlet he wrote near the end of his life — cancer-stricken in wartime London — concluding that humanity had run its course. He died the following August, in 1946.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but usually torn from its meaning
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Wells is correct. What travels falsely is the tone: the line is lifted from a book of near-total despair and re-sold as brisk business-motivation.

items.why: Wells really wrote it in The Mind at the End of its Tether ↗ (1945). Popular copies lower-case “Nature’s” and quote it as an upbeat maxim; the original capital “Nature’s” sits inside a grim argument that humanity faces “steeply up or steeply down” — and Wells bet on down.

items.scope: the adjacent “survival of the most adaptable” myth
items.why: A separate adaptation aphorism — “It is not the strongest… but the most adaptable” — is widely mis-pinned on Darwin; Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to a 1963 lecture by Leon C. Megginson. It is easily confused with the genuine Wells line, but the two are unrelated.

misattribution.truthLine: So: really Wells, verified in his 1945 final book ↗ — just remember he meant it as a warning, not a pep talk.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Mind at the End of its Tether was Wells’s last book, published in 1945 as the Second World War closed. Writing in his late seventies, ill and worn down, the great prophet of scientific progress reversed course: he now argued that reality itself had turned hostile to humankind, and that “the end of everything we call life is close at hand.”

Read in that setting, “Adapt or perish” is not a motivational slogan but the pitiless law Wells believed the species was about to fail. The irony is that the sentence has outlived its author’s pessimism, endlessly re-quoted in boardrooms and self-help as a call to nimble optimism.
context.pull: He meant it as a verdict on humanity’s odds — not a slogan for quarterly planning.
